A plural history of AI ethics, 1950–2025

This is a selective map of retrospective connections, not a linear genealogy and not a ranking of founders.

Keys 1–7 switch tabs · hover or focus a name for more

Problems travel across traditions

Start from contested problems rather than a canon of people. The same text may speak to more than one problem, and the same problem takes different forms in different settings.

A teaching map: links indicate shared problems, not direct influence. Hover or focus a name for the full reference and the register's reading note.

Thirteen lecture anchors across five histories

These focal texts provide an entry into the longer history. They are a deliberate teaching selection, not an authoritative canon or a claim that one tradition led to another.

Ringed marks are lecture anchors. Hover or focus one for its full reference and reading note. Dates identify publications, not the origin of a problem or tradition.

Four questions that still structure debate

These are interpretive prompts for discussion, not summaries that exhaust the texts.

WEIZENBAUM · 1966

When does a machine appear to understand?

ELIZA made visible the gap between an apparently responsive conversation and the procedures that generate it—and the interpretive work people contribute themselves.

What changes when contemporary systems produce more convincing language?

SUCHMAN · 1987

Can a plan stand in for situated action?

Accounts of intelligent systems can mistake formal plans for the practical, contingent activity through which people make sense of a situation.

Whose situation disappears when an automated system treats a plan as complete?

FRIEDMAN & NISSENBAUM · 1996

Where does bias enter a system?

Bias is not only a fault in a model. It can be inherited from social arrangements, introduced through technical choices, or emerge in a new context of use.

What would it take to locate responsibility rather than merely identify unequal outcomes?

MATTHIAS · 2004

Who answers for learning systems?

As systems act in ways their designers cannot fully anticipate, familiar conditions for assigning responsibility can break down.

Does a “responsibility gap” name a missing person, a legal problem, or a problem in how institutions are organized?

Dates identify publications, not the origin of a problem.

Continuities do not erase historical change

The historical value of the earlier texts is not that they predict the present. They help distinguish recurring problems from new infrastructures, scales, and political arrangements.

Persistent questions

Delegated judgement
What happens when consequential decisions are organized through technical systems?
Work and power
Who gains control, income, discretion, or surveillance capacity through automation?
Classification and exclusion
How do categories, predictions, and information systems distribute access and disadvantage?
Responsibility
Who can be called to account when actions are distributed among people and systems?
Human interpretation
What do people supply when they treat a machine's output as meaningful, knowledgeable, or social?

Changed conditions

Scale
Data, deployment, and infrastructural reach operate across populations rather than bounded local systems.
Political economy
Platforms, cloud infrastructure, venture finance, and concentrated corporate power reshape who governs technical change.
Forms of labor
Data work, content moderation, platform work, and automated management make older labor questions newly concrete.
Public governance
Regulation, standards, audits, procurement, and civil-society contestation increasingly define the field.
Generative systems
New capacities and public uptake change the urgency of older questions without settling them.

A selective map of retrospective connections, not a linear genealogy.

Two ways to order 2010–2025

How you organise the field decides which continuities you see. By lineage, a problem can be followed from 1950 to 2025. By track, the same 38 entries show what kind of activity made up the field — and everything before 2010 drops out of view.

Hover for significance and contestation; select for the full record. Entries are documented events, not origins. Position: date and grouping · colour: lineage · shape: track · nothing encodes importance — no citation counts or rankings.

About this pack

What the visuals can show, what they cannot, and where every mark and note comes from.

What this pack can show

  • A problem followed through time. In the lineage ordering of tab v, a concern can be traced from a text of the 1950s to a case or ruling of the 2020s. The connection is a teaching connection made in retrospect, not a claim of influence.
  • What kind of activity made up the field after 2010. The track ordering groups the same entries as scholarship, cases and controversies, institutions and publics, and governance.
  • That the ordering decides the continuity. Switching between the two orderings shows the same entries producing different histories.
  • The boundaries of the selection itself. A lane with no ancestors, and a lane with no post-2010 entry, are visible as such rather than filled.
  • A route into the evidence. Every post-2010 entry names its actors, states what is contested, and gives a primary and two secondary sources to open.

What it cannot show

  • Importance or influence. Nothing encodes prominence: no citation counts, rankings, sizes or emphasis. Two marks in one lane are not a line of descent.
  • Completeness. Thirteen anchors, 41 register works and 38 post-2010 entries are a deliberate selection shaped by what is documented and accessible.
  • Absence as a fact about the world. An empty lane records how the register and the dataset were built, not that nothing happened.
  • Settled interpretation. One sentence cannot resolve the disagreements around a case, a ruling or a departure; read the sources.

This timeline is a teaching map, not a neutral inventory of the history of AI ethics. It selects events, institutions, texts and conflicts that are comparatively documentable in sources accessible to the research team. That selection makes some connections visible while leaving others thin, uncertain or absent. The most important use of this note is therefore methodological: it names the conditions under which a timeline can look more comprehensive, more coherent and more settled than the history it represents.

Selection is an argument, not a discovery procedure

The entries were chosen because they reorganise a concept, make a harm politically consequential, establish an institution or governance practice, contest authority over technical futures, or connect cautiously to an older problem history. These criteria do not remove judgement. They privilege events that leave an accessible public record and that can be rendered in a short caption with a primary source and independent secondary support. Quiet accommodation, everyday repair, informal organising, refusal that never became public, and harms that were normalised rather than contested will be less visible.

Nor does a four-track structure describe four separate worlds. Scholarship can be a form of organising. Litigation can produce concepts. Journalism can create a public. Corporate documentation can be both a governance device and a public-relations intervention. The tracks are teaching aids for comparison, not a theory of causation. An entry's location on one track should not be read as a verdict about what mattered most.

Archive, access and language shape the evidence

The map is disproportionately shaped by English-language materials, open web archives, well-resourced legal systems and institutions that publish stable documents. A court decision, a major newspaper investigation, a conference archive or a formal policy text is easier to cite than oral testimony, community knowledge, materials in languages unavailable to the researchers, precarious worker communication or records held behind paywalls and security restrictions. This is an archival inequality, not evidence that the former matters more.

The geographic distribution of entries should be read in the same way. Including India, Kenya, the Netherlands, international Indigenous data-governance work, Palestine/Israel and UNESCO does not make the timeline global. It only prevents a narrower story from passing as universal. Large parts of Africa, Latin America, West Asia, South Asia, East and Southeast Asia, the Pacific, Eastern Europe and Indigenous territories remain underrepresented. So do linguistic communities whose experiences of training data, language technologies and platform moderation are poorly represented in English research infrastructure.

A further difficulty concerns security and danger. In border control, policing, war, migration, labour and welfare administration, people may be unable safely to document a system, challenge a decision or identify themselves publicly. Secrecy, non-disclosure agreements, inaccessible procurement systems and proprietary claims can make the infrastructure least open to scrutiny precisely where stakes are highest. Absence from the archive cannot be treated as absence from the history.

The category “AI” is historically unstable

Some included systems are not AI in a narrow contemporary technical sense. SyRI and Ofqual, for example, belong because disputes about automated classification, statistical decision systems and administrative infrastructure shaped the conditions in which AI ethics became meaningful. Labelling every data system AI would erase important technical and institutional differences. Refusing to include adjacent systems would imply a false boundary between machine learning and the administrative systems from which it draws data, authority and harms.

The timeline therefore treats “AI ethics” as a contested historical formation rather than a fixed object. It asks how older problems were reassembled under changing technical and institutional conditions. It does not claim that an older debate directly caused a later one unless a source documents that connection. Similarity, recurrence and retrospective usefulness are not evidence of influence.

A timeline compresses disagreement

One sentence can describe a legal ruling, an audit or a worker action. It cannot settle the disagreements surrounding it. The COMPAS controversy includes disputes about methods and fairness criteria. Corporate departures involve conflicting accounts of employment decisions. Generative-AI lawsuits involve allegations, partial rulings and unresolved legal questions. Reporting on military AI can rely on anonymous sources and may be publicly contested. Governance principles may be ambitious yet non-binding. Laws may be enacted yet weakly enforced.

For this reason, captions distinguish what a source documents from an interpretation of its significance. Students should open the linked primary sources, compare independent accounts and ask what each source can support. A timeline should lead into evidence work, not replace it.

The danger of retrospective canonisation

Once a sequence is displayed from 2010 to 2025, it can appear to culminate naturally in foundation models, international regulation or a handful of famous concepts. That appearance is misleading. Contemporary prominence is not proof that an event was decisive at the time, that it travelled across contexts, or that it deserves to represent a field. Citation counts, elite venues and corporate visibility are particularly poor proxies for political importance.

The timeline also risks converting critique into a canon of named texts and institutions. That would repeat the field's tendency to treat affected communities as sources of cases and researchers, firms or regulators as sources of theory. The map counters this only partially by including organising, journalism, worker disputes and litigation. It should be revised with community-produced sources, local histories, non-English materials and accounts of repair and refusal.

How to use the map responsibly

Treat every entry as a proposition open to revision. Ask whose account establishes the event, which actors are named as agents, what is missing from the available record, and whether the caption mistakes a formal commitment for material change. Add local cases and sources in the languages relevant to the class. Pair each high-profile event with a less visible infrastructure or labour history. Keep an exclusion log recording candidates that were rejected because sources were inaccessible, claims could not be verified, or the relation to AI was too weak.

The value of this timeline lies not in completeness. It lies in making its choices, evidentiary limits and political absences inspectable. A plural history of AI ethics must remain revisable, because the conditions under which its archives are made and its futures are contested remain unequal.

The data

  • Post-2010 entries. 38 rows with 19 fields each, read from lecture/post2010/post2010_timeline_csv.csv when this file is built. Each has a primary source and two secondary sources. 32 are dated to the month; 6 to the year only, and those are placed mid-year.
  • Tracks were assigned by the dataset's compilers: Scholarship and concepts 4; Cases and controversies 13; Institutions and publics 8; Governance and infrastructure 13.
  • Lineages are an interpretive assignment, proposed while preparing this pack and approved by the lecturer. Each entry has one lineage; 19 also carry a second. Automation & labor 6; Machine intelligence & interaction 1; Computer ethics & accountability 15; Classification, bias & visibility 12; Artificial agency & moral status 0; No pre-2010 lineage in the register 4. The 4 entries marked as having no pre-2010 lineage record problems for which the ancestor register has no counterpart.
  • Researcher notes exist for all 38 entries. They record verification still needed before quotation, so they are shown only through the lecturer switch in tab v and never printed.
  • Pre-2010 works. The thirteen anchors of tab ii and the works of tab i come from the project's ancestor register (41 works). Hovers give the full reference and, for 27 of them, a reading note stating the distinction the work made. Reading note from the project's ancestor register — drafted in the project, not yet reviewed by the lecturer.
  • Time axis. In tab v the scale changes at 2010: ten years per column before, one year per column after, marked on the axis. Before 2010 the chart is sparse by design, not by lack of history.
  • Encoding. Position encodes date and grouping; colour encodes lineage; shape encodes track (circle scholarship, triangle cases, square institutions, diamond governance). Neither size nor colour encodes prominence.

Rebuilding

This file is generated. Edit the sources, then run python3 lecture/build_lecture_pack.py. It opens from disk and needs no network.

A lecture aid. Verify any quotation or expanded claim against the primary source before presenting it.
